new_statements.translation: [p.85] The two parties, we conclude, each carried their own peculiarities into the language as they used it - their speech sounds, their syllable accent, their length system and their manner of stressing - or at best achieved only an imperfect imitation of the foreign pronunciation aimed at. The sound side of the language therefore had to be strongly fluctuating [...] [p.89] Such spellings can consequently now and then help to establish the place of the stressed syllable in the Russenorsk word in question. [...] A uniform or even reasonably clear picture simply cannot be obtained in this area. In one case it is the Norwegian, in the other the Russian pronunciation system that probably underlies or underlay the form

new_statements.rule_in_words: No pidgin-internal stress rule: each side (Pomor Russians, North Norwegians) pronounced Russenorsk words with its own native accentuation and quantity system, so stress placement fluctuated by speaker and by the etymon's source language; the written record (Norwegian orthography, occasional Qvigstad stress marks) lets stress be fixed only for scattered individual words, and Broch states that no uniform picture of stress can be obtained.
new_statements.exceptions: Ad hoc word notes only: ['sabagof] 'boots' (Russ. gen.pl. sapogóv) recorded 'with striking stress' (p.94); klæba 'bread' first-syllable-stressed per Reusch but otherwise in the material (p.109 n.1); ligge ne beside Reusch's end-stressed 'liggné', 'both forms probably in use' (p.109 n.2); occasional pretonic vowel length ([kā-'pītan]-type forms) attributed to Russian pronunciation habits (pp.88-89). Broch & Jahr 1984 (not opened) mention 'trykk på siste stavelse' once (scan p.45), evidently for a particular item.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern word forms as written down by (mostly Norwegian) collectors; Broch separates Norwegian-mouth and Russian-mouth pronunciation; sentence intonation is mentioned separately only for yes/no questions ('bare gjennem tonefaldet', p.101).
new_statements.identity_note: Russenorsk proper (russ1267), the Pomor-trade pidgin of Finnmark/Troms, recorded almost entirely from Norwegian writers c. 1800-1920s; Broch 1927 explicitly distinguishes the Norwegian-mouth and Russian-mouth renderings and treats neither as a norm. No dialect issue beyond the two ethnolects.

sources.note: Sections 4-6 (pp. 85-89) treat sounds, quantity and stress: each party (Russians, Norwegians) carried its own syllable accent, length system and manner of stressing into the pidgin, so the sound side was 'strongly fluctuating'; stress position of individual RN words can only now and then be fixed from spellings, and 'a uniform or reasonably clear picture cannot be obtained at all in this area' because now the Norwegian, now the Russian pronunciation system underlies a form.
